intro: This page maps common public claims to what Illustrative Manuscripts actually contains — open CNTR transcriptions, a bounded 1–400 CE Greek NT slice, and hand-curated Qurʾān catalog data. It is meant to help students, researchers, debaters, and apologists stay precise: neither inflating our counts nor pretending the site settles every tradition-scale debate.

pathways.title: Student
pathways.description: Learn how to read a witness card, what our numbers mean, and where block-level famous passages differ from the word census.

pathways.title: Researcher / academic
pathways.description: Download the open census, read methodology, and cite CNTR/INTF for primaries — cite us for the illustrative collation slice only.

pathways.title: Debater / apologist
pathways.description: Check claim discipline before arguing from our charts — then use Famous passages, Variants, Uthmanic rasm, and Coverage honesty together.

claims.claim: Nobody has counted New Testament variants.
claims.why: Peter Gurry (NTS 2016) estimates on the order of ~500,000 readings across the whole Greek tradition — a extrapolation, not a hand count of every manuscript. Our site does publish a mechanical count, but only for word-aligned disagreements vs SR GNT in extant letters of our 1–400 CE CNTR witness slice — not the full ~5,700+ manuscript tradition.

scholarship.label: Gurry 2016 — How Many Variants Are in the Greek New Testament?

claims.claim: The New Testament text is completely unknown before late manuscripts.
claims.why: Within our frozen window, substantial Greek material survives from the second and third centuries (papyri) plus fourth-century codices such as 01 and 03. That does not recover every verse in every book from every century — but it falsifies the blanket claim that nothing early exists.

claims.claim: By about 400 CE the Greek New Testament text is largely recoverable.
claims.why: Standard critical-edition framing (and our site’s own scope statement) treats the fourth-century major codices plus earlier papyri as the backbone for reconstructing the Greek text — while still not counting every later Byzantine variant or replacing NA28/ECM apparatus judgments.

claims.claim: P66, P75, 01, and 03 lack the Pericope Adulterae (John 7:53–8:11).
claims.why: In CNTR transcriptions in our corpus, that block is marked absent; narrative runs from 7:52 to 8:12 in those witnesses. Later Byzantine copies insert the pericope — a different story from our early slice.

claims.claim: Mark originally ended at 16:8 in the earliest complete Greek codices in our window.
claims.why: Codex Sinaiticus (01) and Codex Vaticanus (03) end Mark at 16:8 in the main Greek tradition represented in CNTR; the longer ending 16:9–20 is a later supplement in the manuscript record. Textual critics still debate composition history — our data support the codex-level statement for 01/03.

claims.claim: The Comma Johanneum is in the earliest Greek tradition.
claims.why: 1 John 5:7–8 is extant in early Greek witnesses with the short reading (Spirit, water, blood). The explicit heavenly Trinity wording of the Comma is not attested in Greek before the sixteenth century; it entered some Latin lines and late Greek retro-translations.

claims.claim: The Qurʾān has no manuscript variation.
claims.why: The Uthmanic Text Type is highly uniform, but published stemmatics (Cook; Sidky; van Putten) report on the order of ~35–40 regional rasm differences among the four ʿUthmānic exemplar traditions — not wholesale content rewrites, but not zero graphic variation. Early palimpsests such as Ṣanʿāʾ 1 preserve a lower text that is not UT.

scholarship.label: Cook — The Koran: A Very Short Introduction (regional rasm overview)

claims.claim: From about 650 CE the Uthmanic text type is already stable.
claims.why: Sidky and van Putten’s archetype framing treats UT as stable from the seventh century onward for the rasm tradition they model — while allowing later scribal noise and regional graphic differences, not a claim of byte-identical copies everywhere.

claims.claim: Illustrative Manuscripts proves intentional theological corruption at scale.
claims.why: Optional intentional-vs-error tags on some Greek NT units are heuristic and model-assisted — useful for exploration, not proof of motive across the tradition. Most counted units are spelling, word order, or ordinary scribal difference vs SR GNT.

links.label: Cite & learn — what we are not claiming

claims.claim: Our census equals the NA28 apparatus or all Greek manuscripts.
claims.why: Out of scope by design: we mechanically align a bounded CNTR witness set to SR GNT. NA28/ECM/IGNTP record editorial judgments and thousands of witnesses beyond our 1–400 CE illustrative slice.
